issue: Trivially weak JWT secret used in local development environment
recommendation: Replace with a long, high-entropy random string (>=32 bytes from crypto.randomBytes). Even in dev, weak secrets train bad habits and risk leaking to prod via copy/paste. .env is in .gitignore which is correct; verify the secret was never committed to git history (git log -S 'abc123' returned no commits — confirmed).

issue: Hardcoded MCP API key fallback used if MCP_API_KEY env var is unset
recommendation: Fail fast at startup if MCP_API_KEY is unset (throw Error). The current fallback ships a publicly-readable static API key in source — anyone reading the repo (this is committed) can call set_feature_state / adjust_traffic_rollout via the HTTP transport. Rotate this token immediately and audit git history. Also: line 128 logs the key to stdout (`console.log(\`API key: ${API_KEY}\`)`).

issue: MCP API key written to server stdout on startup
recommendation: Never log secrets. Remove this line; if you must show that the server is auth-ready, log only the SHA-256 prefix or 'API key loaded (length=N)'. In production logs/log aggregators, this is a credential leak.

issue: API key comparison uses non-constant-time string equality (timing attack)
recommendation: Use crypto.timingSafeEqual with Buffer.from(token) and Buffer.from(API_KEY). The current `!==` short-circuits on first differing byte, leaking the prefix one byte at a time over many requests. Tools like sleeper can derive the key remotely. Also: there is no rate-limit on /mcp, so an attacker can issue millions of probes.

issue: POST /api/users/login has no rate-limit middleware — unbounded credential stuffing
recommendation: Wrap with express-rate-limit (e.g. 5 attempts / 15 min per IP) or an account-lockout strategy. Same applies to POST /api/users (registration) which can be abused to enumerate emails (different status codes: 400 'User already exists' vs 201).

issue: IDOR — getOrderById has no ownership check; any authenticated user can read any order including shipping address, items, and payer email
evidence: const order = await Order.findById(req.params.id).populate('user','name email'); if (order) { res.json(order) }
recommendation: Add an ownership check before returning: if (order.user._id.toString() !== req.user._id.toString() && !req.user.isAdmin) { res.status(403); throw new Error('Forbidden') }. As currently written, knowing or brute-forcing any 24-hex ObjectId lets a normal user fetch another user's order with PII (email, shipping address).

issue: updateOrderToPaid has no ownership check and trusts client-supplied PayPal payment result without server-side verification
evidence: order.paymentResult = { id: req.body.id, status: req.body.status, update_time: req.body.update_time, email_address: req.body.payer.email_address }
owasp: A01 Broken Access Control / A08 Data Integrity Failures
recommendation: (1) Verify order.user equals req.user._id. (2) Independently verify the PayPal transaction with PayPal's API using the supplied transaction id — never trust the client's claim that status='COMPLETED'. As-is, any authenticated user can mark any order as paid by POSTing crafted JSON to /api/orders/:anyOrderId/pay.

issue: Order totals (itemsPrice, taxPrice, shippingPrice, totalPrice) accepted from client without server-side recomputation
evidence: const { orderItems, ..., itemsPrice, taxPrice, shippingPrice, totalPrice } = req.body; const order = new Order({ ..., itemsPrice, taxPrice, shippingPrice, totalPrice })
recommendation: Recompute every price field server-side from the canonical product documents fetched by orderItems[].product. The current code lets an attacker submit totalPrice=0 (or negative) and bypass payment. This is a classic eCommerce price-tampering vulnerability.

issue: User-controlled regex passed directly to MongoDB $regex — NoSQL injection / ReDoS
recommendation: Escape regex metacharacters before passing to $regex (e.g. keyword.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')), or use a $text index with $search. Without escaping, `?keyword=(a+)+$` causes catastrophic backtracking (denial of service) and `?keyword=.*` returns the entire catalog bypassing pagination semantics.

issue: No security hardening middleware (helmet, cors policy, body-size limit) on Express app
evidence: app.use(express.json()) — no helmet, no rate-limit, no CORS allowlist, no body-size cap
recommendation: Add helmet() for default security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options, HSTS, etc.). Add express.json({ limit: '100kb' }) to cap body size and prevent JSON-bomb DoS. Although the SPA is same-origin in prod, a missing CORS allowlist becomes a footgun when the API is later split off.

issue: Error stack returned to client in non-production environments
recommendation: OK in dev only — confirm NODE_ENV is reliably set to 'production' in every deployed environment. A missing/typoed NODE_ENV (e.g. 'Production', 'prod') causes stack traces (file paths, library versions) to leak in production responses. Use strict whitelist === 'production'; default to safe behaviour otherwise (current code already does this — but flag here as a fragile reliance on a single env var).

issue: JWT lifetime is 30 days with no refresh/rotation mechanism; combined with localStorage storage gives an attacker a long-lived bearer credential
owasp: A04 Insecure Design / A07 Authentication Failures
recommendation: Shorten to 15–60 minutes and add a refresh-token rotation flow stored in an httpOnly secure cookie. Per CLAUDE.md the team is aware tokens live in localStorage (XSS-readable) — 30d half-life makes XSS impact catastrophic. ADR-003 selected JWT-vs-session; revisit token TTL there.

issue: File upload validates only filename extension and MIME (both attacker-controlled); no size limit and no content sniffing
evidence: filetypes = /jpg|jpeg|png/; const extname = filetypes.test(path.extname(...)); const mimetype = filetypes.test(file.mimetype); const upload = multer({ storage, fileFilter })
recommendation: (1) Set multer({ limits: { fileSize: 2 * 1024 * 1024 } }) — without this, an attacker can fill the disk with one giant request. (2) Sniff the actual file magic bytes (file-type pkg) instead of trusting client-supplied MIME. (3) Sanitise filename — currently `${file.fieldname}-${Date.now()}${path.extname(file.originalname)}` could be exploited if originalname contains traversal (e.g. '../../etc/passwd.jpg' — path.extname returns '.jpg' so partial mitigation, but defence-in-depth requires sanitisation). (4) Endpoint is unauthenticated — anyone can POST to /api/upload.

issue: POST /api/upload has no authentication or authorization middleware
recommendation: Wrap with protect + admin (matches the rest of admin-only product flows). As-is, anonymous users can upload arbitrary jpg/png files to the server's uploads/ directory and consume disk space (no size limit either). The endpoint also echoes back the saved path, enabling reconnaissance of the upload directory structure.

issue: bcrypt cost factor of 10 is below modern recommendation (12+)
evidence: const salt = await bcrypt.genSalt(10); this.password = await bcrypt.hash(this.password, salt)
recommendation: Bump to genSalt(12) or genSalt(14). Cost 10 was the OWASP recommendation circa 2015; on modern hardware (2026) GPU-accelerated cracking makes 10 insufficient. Argon2id is the preferred algorithm if you can take the dependency.

issue: Severely outdated dependencies with known CVEs
recommendation: jsonwebtoken <9.0.0 has CVE-2022-23529 (RCE via crafted token when secretOrPublicKey is a function — not directly exploitable here but still HIGH severity in the package). multer 1.x has CVE-2022-24434 (DoS via crafted boundary, fixed in 1.4.4-lts.1; major upgrade to 2.x recommended). mongoose 5.x is end-of-life (no security patches since 2024). Run `npm audit` and update; mongoose upgrade requires removing useCreateIndex per backend/CLAUDE.md.

issue: No password complexity policy on registration / update
evidence: Registration accepts any password (e.g. seeder uses '123456'); no length check, no character-class check, no breach-list check.
recommendation: Validate password server-side: min length 12, reject the top-1000 breached passwords (zxcvbn or HaveIBeenPwned k-anonymity API). Sample seed data uses '123456' which is fine for fixtures but indicates the absence of any policy.

issue: Failed JWT verification logs full error to console but does not record a security event (audit log)
evidence: } catch (error) { console.error(error); res.status(401); throw new Error('Not authorized, token failed') }
recommendation: Emit a structured audit log entry (timestamp, ip, user-agent, partial token id) to a dedicated security log when JWT verification fails. console.error to stdout makes detection of token-stuffing attacks impossible at scale. Same applies to admin-only routes that return 401 to non-admins (no record of attempted privilege escalation).

issue: GET /api/feature-flags/:name is Public — leaks feature-flag names, status, and rollout strategy to unauthenticated users
recommendation: Decide whether per-flag status is a public concern. If the flag system is used for canary releases of unreleased features (the description fields in features.json contain detailed engineering notes — e.g. 'Stripe webhook bug'), the response is a reconnaissance gift. Restrict to authenticated users or expose only minimal information (true/false for the calling user).

issue: Path-parameter from URL is used as object key lookup without validation — allows prototype-pollution-style probes (__proto__, constructor) and arbitrary key probing
evidence: const flag = flags[req.params.name]; if (!flag) { res.status(404); throw new Error(`Feature flag '${req.params.name}' not found`) }
recommendation: Validate req.params.name against an allowlist or regex (e.g. /^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{1,40}$/) before object lookup. Also: the error message echoes the raw user input — combined with verbose stack traces in non-prod environments, this is reflected-data territory.

issue: Server-side fetch to user-configurable OLLAMA_URL — partial SSRF surface if env var is attacker-influenced
evidence: const res = await fetch(`${OLLAMA_URL}/api/embed`, { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ model: OLLAMA_MODEL, input: [text] }) })
recommendation: Low risk because OLLAMA_URL is operator-set, not request-derived. Flagging for defence-in-depth: if this MCP server is ever deployed in a multi-tenant environment, validate OLLAMA_URL against an allowlist of expected hosts at startup. The query text itself is also forwarded to the embedding service — review whether sending user input to a third-party model is acceptable per privacy policy.

issue: JWT verify does not pin the signing algorithm — accepts whatever alg is in the token header (alg=none historical risk)
recommendation: Pass { algorithms: ['HS256'] } as the third argument to jwt.verify. jsonwebtoken 8.x is patched against alg=none and alg-confusion (RS256→HS256 with pubkey-as-secret) by default, but explicit pinning is a defence-in-depth requirement and survives library downgrades.
